about: Phrases and habits that make marketing copy read as machine-written or as a press release. Each has the reason it fails and the fix. Errors block approval in the UMS queue; warnings do not. Keep entries specific: a word only lands here when it is filler in almost every marketing sentence it appears in.

phrases.why: Nobody says this out loud about an app.
phrases.fix: Name the thing the person can now do.
Say what changes, with a number or a before and after.

phrases.why: Every product claims it, so it reads as nothing.
phrases.fix: Show the step that used to hurt and is now gone.

phrases.why: Hype the reader has learned to skip.
phrases.fix: State the one specific difference and let them judge.

phrases.why: The opening line of a thousand generated posts.
phrases.fix: Open on the person, the problem or the result.

phrases.why: Words that mark text as machine-written.

phrases.fix: Use, run, cut, ship, save: the concrete verb.
Replace with proof: a benchmark, a clip, a customer's words.

phrases.why: The reader cares what it is, not how you feel.
phrases.fix: Lead with the thing. Feelings can go in the reply.
Open with the moment the problem happens.

phrases.why: Engagement-bait cadence that X and LinkedIn readers now scroll past.
phrases.fix: Cut the line. If the point is strong it does not need the drumroll.

phrases.why: Abstract and grand where the product is small and real.
Says nothing about what it does.
phrases.fix: Name the two or three jobs it does.

match: at the end of the day
phrases.fix: End on the call to action or the strongest line.

phrases.why: Urgency with no reason given reads as a scam; a false deadline can also be a deceptive practice.
phrases.fix: Give the real reason and the real date, or drop it.

phrases.why: A claim that needs substantiation and, for health or money, can break advertising law.
phrases.fix: Only keep it with a source you can show; otherwise state what you can prove.

patterns.why: The "not just X, it's Y" construction is the most recognised generated-copy pattern.
Three one-word sentences in a row ("Fast. Simple. Yours.") reads as template copy.
patterns.fix: One real sentence with a specific.

patterns.regex: ^(ever wondered|have you ever|what if i told you|are you tired of|struggling with)
patterns.why: Question openers that the reader answers "no" to and scrolls.
Three or more em dashes in one post is a strong generated-text signal.
A wall of hashtags at the end looks like spam and most platforms no longer reward it.
patterns.fix: Keep three to five that describe the post.
Sentence case. Emphasis comes from the claim.
